meta.title: Events and middleware
meta.description: What runs before an interaction and can cancel it, what reports it afterwards, and the order the two happen in.

basics.intro: There are two kinds of callback. handlers are middleware: they run before the component acts and decide whether it acts at all. The onX props are events: they report what has already happened. Anything that needs to intervene — a confirmation, an unsaved change, a permission — belongs in the first; anything that needs to record or react belongs in the second.
basics.next: A middleware receives the context and a next function. Calling it runs the default behavior and then the events; not calling it cancels both. The context is read-only, and next may be called later — after an await, for instance — in which case the default behavior runs then, provided the component is still mounted.

order.intro: For one interaction, in this order:
rows: The middleware for that interaction, if you gave one.
The component’s own behavior, if the middleware called next.
The state callbacks: onViewChange, onDateChange, onOpenItemIdChange and their kind.
The domain events: onItemOpen, onNavigate, onOverflowOpen and their kind.
order.frames: The events that come from scrolling — onActiveShiftChange, onHeaderExpandedChange, onPinnedChange — fire at most once per animation frame, and only when the value actually changed.

middleware.intro: The eleven middleware, generated from the package’s declarations:

points: A cancelled interaction leaves focus where it was: nothing moves because something did not happen.
A middleware that opens a confirmation of your own is responsible for its focus; the component has not moved any.
Because the events report rather than decide, a screen reader never hears about something the middleware went on to cancel.
handlers holds every middleware; each one is optional.
The imperative handle skips the middleware on purpose: it is your own call, not the reader’s.
Events are ordinary props, so they compose with whatever state library you already use.
The middleware context is read-only: it cannot change the item, the target shift or the sort. To change the outcome, cancel and then act through the imperative handle.
An asynchronous next that resolves after the component unmounted does nothing, silently.
There is no single event that fires for every interaction; each one has its own.
